Executive Summary  
The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) published the first National Energy Demand 
Strategy (NEDS) Decision in July 2024 (CRU202467) with the aim of enhancing Ireland’s energy 
demand flexibility in a coordinated phased manner to support a more sustainable, cost-effective, 
and secure energy system. 
This Annual Update demonstrates that the NEDS implementation is progressing well, with a 
majority of actions now delivered or on track, while recognising that delivery is increasingly 
complex and requires strengthened coordination across Government, regulators and system 
operators. 
This publication is the third NEDS update, with one further update expected in this series to close 
out the NEDS implementation phase in due course. 
Since the previous NEDS update was published in July 2025, an additional 18 actions have been 
completed, bringing the total number to 34 of 53 actions delivered to date. At the same time, the 
CRU has undertaken a structured review of delivery timelines, resulting in the rebaselining of 16 
actions to reflect evolving policy, market, and operational dependencies. This rebaselining reflects 
a maturing implementation phase, as NEDS actions become more closely integrated with wider 
national and European policy developments.

A number of key developments have advanced since the previous update: 
• 
Large Energy Users Action Plan (LEAP), approved by Government in January 2026, 
establishes a coordinated national approach to planning and enabling large-scale demand 
growth, including the development of green energy parks and associated infrastructure;

4 
 
• 
Continued progress in the National Smart Metering Programme, with over 2.1 million 
meters installed, supporting the rollout of smart tariffs and data-enabled services; 
• 
Advancement of flexibility market frameworks, including ESBN’s demand flexibility 
procurement and EirGrid’s Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES) programme; 
• 
Ongoing development of the Flexibility Needs Assessment (FNA) under ACER, which 
will play a central role in setting future flexibility targets and may inform the evolution of 
NEDS in the medium term. 
Stakeholder feedback, gathered through the online NEDS Review Survey (February 2026), 
indicates strong support for the direction of the strategy, with particular recognition of progress in 
smart metering, flexibility procurement, and large user policy. However, stakeholders emphasised 
the need to accelerate delivery of dynamic tariffs, network tariff reform, and customer participation 
measures, alongside improved programme coordination. 
Looking ahead, the next phase of NEDS implementation will require a more integrated, 
cross-government approach. The scale and complexity of demand growth — particularly from 
Large Energy Users (LEUs) — and the increasing interaction with EU frameworks (including the 
FNA and Demand Response Network Code) mean that future strategy development will need to 
extend beyond the CRU’s remit alone. 
The CRU will continue to monitor the delivery of flexibility through the NEDS, including through 
the forthcoming Demand Flexibility Forecasting Report 2026: NEDS Action 0.3 (CRU202629), 
while engaging with Government Departments on the future direction and governance of a next 
iteration of the strategy.

5 
 
Public / Customer Impact Statement  
 
The CRU launched the National Energy Demand Strategy (NEDS) in July 2024 in response to the 
Government’s Climate Action Plan 2023 (CAP23) to enhance Ireland’s energy demand flexibility 
with a view to supporting a more sustainable, cost-effective, and secure energy system. In 
essence, if a high proportion of customers can shift their energy consumption to times when there 
is a significant quantity of electricity being generated by renewable generation, customers can 
benefit and reductions in carbon emissions can be achieved, even as overall demand for energy 
increases. 
Demand flexibility enables and empowers energy customers to increase their use of renewable 
energy whilst also reducing demand during times of high-carbon intensity on the energy system. 
This ability to adjust consumption patterns in response to fluctuations in renewable energy output 
and network conditions is crucial to decarbonising Ireland’s energy system and in the long term 
will result in a major change to how the energy system operates and in how customers organise 
their energy usage, from domestic households to businesses and large industrial users of energy.   
The NEDS decision identified 532 high impact, short-term actions and 3 Government Department 
recommendations. Following the publication of the strategy, the NEDS entered its implementation 
phase. To ensure that a transparent, coordinated, and collaborative approach was ultimately 
adopted towards the implementation of the NEDS, the CRU committed to publishing a series of 
updates in order to monitor and provide an ongoing summary of progress and status updates on 
NEDS actions, recommendations, and relevant policy developments. This update is the third of 
such updates that have been published by the CRU to date with one further update expected in 
this series to close out the NEDS implementation phase in due course.

1. Progress and associated updates  
1.1 Introduction 
This NEDS publication is the third in a series of NEDS updates that the CRU has delivered since 
the NEDS Decision (CRU202467) was published in July 2024. The purpose of this update is to 
provide a clear view of delivery progress, key developments and emerging challenges, as NEDS 
transitions from initial implementation into a more mature delivery phase.  
While the first two NEDS updates were published on a biannual basis, a decision was made to 
transition to an annual basis, which is commensurate with the advancement of the strategy’s 
implementation. 
Since the previous update (July 2025), the context for the NEDS delivery has continued to evolve, 
with significant developments across Government policy (including the Large Energy Users Action 
Plan (LEAP)), regulatory frameworks, and European initiatives such as the Flexibility Needs 
Assessment (FNA). 
This update reflects progress against actions, but also positions that progress within a broader 
and increasingly integrated policy landscape. 
1.2 Policy Context and Strategic Alignment 
1 
Policy Context and Strategic Alignment 
The NEDS sits within a broader and evolving policy landscape at a national and European level, 
aimed at delivering Ireland’s climate, energy, and economic objectives. 
At a national level, the Climate Action Plan (CAP) provides the overarching framework for 
emissions reduction targets and sectoral actions, including the development of demand-side 
flexibility as a key enabler of a decarbonised electricity system. NEDS supports the delivery of 
CAP objectives by identifying and coordinating specific actions required to enable flexibility across 
the energy system. 
More recently, the Large Energy Users Action Plan (LEAP), approved by Government in 
January 2026, establishes a strategic framework for accommodating significant growth in 
electricity demand from energy-intensive sectors, including data centres. LEAP focuses on 
coordinated infrastructure delivery, spatial planning, and enabling large-scale demand-side 
flexibility.

12 
 
There are clear interdependencies between NEDS and LEAP, particularly in relation to LEUs, 
flexibility markets, and network planning. While NEDS focuses on system-wide demand flexibility 
across all customer segments, LEAP provides a more targeted, cross-government approach for 
a specific high-impact demand segment. 
In addition, a number of other national initiatives and policy frameworks interact with NEDS, 
including: 
• 
National Energy Affordability and Transition (NEAT)-related policy development, 
focusing on the distributional and consumer impacts of the energy transition; 
• 
The National Hydrogen Strategy and broader Energy Security Package, which 
influence long-term system planning and the future role of electricity and gas networks; 
• 
Ongoing work on electricity network planning and tariff reform, including the Electricity 
Network Tariff Structure Review. 
At European level, the policy landscape is also evolving. In particular: 
• 
The Flexibility Needs Assessment (FNA), being undertaken in line with ACER 
methodology, will provide a system-wide assessment of Ireland’s future flexibility 
requirements; 
• 
The forthcoming Demand Response Network Code (DRNC) will introduce harmonised 
rules across the EU to enable demand-side participation in electricity markets. 
These European developments are expected to play an increasingly important role in 
shaping the future design of flexibility frameworks in Ireland, and may inform or supersede 
elements of the current NEDS over time. 
Finally, the Programme for Government sets the overarching political and strategic direction, 
including commitments on climate action, energy security, and economic development, which 
underpin the development of NEDS and related initiatives. 
Overall, NEDS operates as a coordinating framework within this wider policy landscape, 
translating high-level climate and energy objectives into actionable steps to enable demand-side 
flexibility, while aligning with parallel initiatives that address infrastructure, large demand growth, 
and market design. 
1.3 NEDS Implementation & Progress 
Since the publication of the previous NEDS update in Q3 2025 (CRU202580), the NEDS 
Implementation Group has continued to oversee and monitor progress against the 53 actions and

13 
 
3 recommendations for Government. This NEDS Implementation Group has continued to convene 
on a quarterly basis, with recent meetings having taken place in October 2025 and March 2026. 
An additional 18 actions have now been completed since the previous NEDS update was 
published in July 2025, bringing the total number to 34 completed NEDS actions to date. This is 
indicative of the continuing further advancement of the implementation of the NEDS, particularly 
as it has been necessary to navigate through a constantly evolving Irish and global energy 
landscape amidst multiple legislative changes and developments, in addition to organisational 
and global challenges.   
A variety of factors and circumstances have arisen during the course of the NEDS implementation, 
resulting in the need to rebaseline the completion dates for some NEDS actions, in order to reflect 
latest developments and updates.  
A rebaselining review has been conducted of eligible NEDS actions to reflect genuine barriers, 
constraints, and/or dependencies encountered by action owners to date. The criteria for 
consideration included: 
- 
Outstanding dependencies, i.e. where inputs are still required from external sources or 
third parties preventing an action from progressing through to completion;  
- 
Immature action framing, scope growth or change, i.e. where developments in the interim 
since the NEDS was first published in July 2024 have led to changes materially impacting 
a NEDS action in a significant way; 
- 
Resources, i.e. where a NEDS action owner may have had insufficient resources resulting 
in an inability to complete the action as per the original target date;  
- 
Priority, i.e. the completion of a NEDS action may not currently be an organisational 
prioritisation for a particular stakeholder due to a variety of potential reasons.  
Following this review, the CRU has revised the completion dates of 16 actions. These are clearly 
identified as such within the NEDS actions update status table provided in Section 5, and also in 
Figure 1 below, where such actions are now depicted as being “on track” relative to the revised 
completion dates that have now been applied. Of these 16 rebaselined actions, 10 are due to be 
completed in 2026 and the rest of the actions have delivery dates further into the future.

1.4 Updates on three NEDS recommendations for 
Government Departments 
The NEDS decision in 2024 outlined three key recommendations for Government Departments, 
particularly DCEE and DETE, to support the implementation of the NEDS. Updates on progress 
that has been made on each of these recommendations to date are summarised below. 
1. Policy measures regarding carbon emissions & SECs (Overall Strategy) 
The first NEDS recommendation highlighted the need for Government Departments to monitor 
the relative contribution of different demand segments to overall carbon emissions, and to 
consider whether further policy measures may be required to support decarbonisation objectives, 
including in the context of Sectoral Emissions Ceilings (SECs). 
Since the publication of the NEDS Decision, engagement has continued between the CRU and 
relevant Government Departments in relation to the role of demand side flexibility in supporting 
emissions reduction targets. This includes consideration of how policy measures, regulatory 
frameworks and market signals can be aligned to support decarbonisation across the electricity 
system. 
Given the cross sectoral nature of emissions policy and its interaction with wider CAP measures, 
this recommendation remains under ongoing active consideration by Government Departments. 
The CRU, in alignment with recommendations outlined on NEDS Action 0.2, will continue to 
engage with relevant stakeholders on this area as part of the broader evolution of NEDS and 
related policy frameworks.

15 
 
2. Enhanced emissions reporting framework - Part 2 (Area 2D: Demand Flexibility & 
Response – Information, Certification and Reporting) 
The second NEDS recommendation relates to the development of an enhanced emissions 
reporting framework, building on existing initiatives and supporting greater transparency in relation 
to electricity related emissions. 
Progress has been made in recent years in establishing the foundations for emissions reporting, 
including through the development of reporting frameworks for LEUs and ongoing work by 
relevant agencies. Further development of this area requires coordination across multiple bodies, 
including Government Departments and agencies with responsibility for emissions data, reporting, 
and policy design. 
In this context, the delivery of a comprehensive emissions reporting framework continues to be 
considered as part of wider Government policy development under the Climate Action Plan.  
The CRU will continue to support this work, including through its role in providing data, regulatory 
insights, and engagement with market participants. 
3. Consider a national strategic approach for the facilitation of new LEU connections 
(Area 3: New Demand Connections)  
The third recommendation related to the need for consideration to be given to a national strategic 
approach for the planning of large demand customers and associated infrastructure requirements 
(e.g. energy, water, broadband, transport etc.), the associated costs and benefits, and any 
potential risks arising from high volumes of similar demand customer types. 
The LEAP was established by DETE and DCEE, and approved by Government in January 2026. 
LEAP seeks to enable Ireland to attract next generation investment across Ireland’s regions in 
energy intensive sectors associated with the greatest future strategic economic opportunities by 
addressing barriers impacting LEU developments, including with energy infrastructure delivery. A 
central pillar of LEAP will be to provide a framework for the establishment of green energy parks 
in which to co-locate the most energy-intensive LEU sectors with the supply of renewables and 
other enabling technologies. It further seeks to unlock increased LEU demand side flexibility 
through the establishment of associated regulatory frameworks and market structures. This ‘plan-
led’ approach will ensure alignment of Ireland’s industrial, climate and energy policies, and 
consistency with other strategic Government priorities.

16 
 
1.5 Large Energy Users Action Plan (LEAP)3 
To deliver on commitments within the Programme for Government, the Large Energy User Action 
Plan (LEAP) was established by Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (DETE) and 
the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE), and approved by Government 
in January 2026. LEAP seeks to enable Ireland to attract next generation investment across 
Ireland’s regions in energy intensive sectors associated with the greatest future strategic 
economic opportunities by addressing barriers impacting LEU developments, including with 
energy infrastructure delivery. It does this, inter alia, by planning spatially for coordinated 
infrastructure delivery, thereby seeking to derisk these complex projects. It further seeks to unlock 
short-term LEU development opportunities through the effective utilisation of existing energy 
infrastructure, led by enhanced demand-side flexibility. This ‘plan-led’ approach will ensure 
alignment of Ireland’s industrial, climate and energy policies, and consistency with other strategic 
Government priorities.  
The implementation of LEAP’s 17 actions will take place across Government, with priority 
workstreams to be led on and supported by Government Departments, the CRU and energy 
system operators (SOs). A central pillar of LEAP will be to provide a framework for the 
establishment of green energy parks in which to co-locate the most energy-intensive LEU sectors 
with the supply of renewables and other enabling technologies. LEAP also seeks to unlock 
increased LEU demand side flexibility through establishment of associated regulatory frameworks 
and market structures. DETE intends for LEAP to act as a core cross-government instrument 
which supports the development of flexibility for a specific high impact demand segment, in 
support of NEDS objectives. The critical interdependencies between LEAP and NEDS are 
recognised.    
1.6 NEDS Review Survey 
The CRU embarked on a review of the NEDS in terms of its design, focus, and progress to assess 
its performance to date. An online survey was published by the CRU in February 2026, which 
forms part of broader stakeholder engagement being undertaken by the CRU to support the 
ongoing implementation of the NEDS.

The input obtained from this survey, particularly common themes that arose in response to 
questions 4 – 6, has helped to inform the CRU to ensure that the NEDS remains responsive, 
inclusive, and impactful.  
 
1.1.1 Common themes on NEDS areas performing well and notable achievements to 
date: 
Stakeholders indicated that progress has been made in NEDS Areas 2 (Demand Flexibility and 
Response) and 3 (New Demand Connections) providing clarity for market participants and 
demand customers, whilst Area 1 (Smart Services) has been delivering essential building blocks 
for the growth of flexibility and shaping of the demand. It was also the view of stakeholders that 
regulatory clarity and commitment are essential in supporting industry investment decisions and 
sustaining momentum for consumers on the journey towards flexibility. Some NEDS workstreams 
of note were as follows: 
 
Smart Metering & Smart Services:  
The 2million+ installs milestone and the Smart Meter Data Access Code were frequently cited 
as necessary building blocks for later-stage flexibility and data-driven services, such as 
dynamic tariffs and automated response. Stakeholders value the clarity and programme 
discipline underpinning this rollout. 
 
Demand Flexibility Procurement:  
ESBN’s local flexibility pilots/procurement and TSO white-paper activity are seen as positive 
market signals and provide confidence to market participants.  
 
Connections Policy:  
Publication of LEU policy and related new demand connections steps are welcomed to give 
pathway clarity.  
 
1.1.2 Common themes on NEDS areas that have made less progress to date or are 
viewed as requiring further adjustment: 
Whilst it was noted that progress has been made across all NEDS areas and the strategy is 
focused on the right direction, stakeholders were of the view that a continued effort to align with 
policies and further developments must be applied to unlock the benefits of the NEDS areas. The 
following in particular were noted:

19 
 
 
Tariffs & Price Signals:   
Stakeholders identified retail dynamic tariffs as being central to unlocking demand-side 
response, and how delays or uncertainty in their delivery creates risk which in turn constrains 
the scale and pace of implicit flexibility. Similarly, stakeholders were of the view that network 
tariff reform must move faster and align with the other price signals in the market to deliver 
the intended result and participation from commercial and LEU customers.  
 
Storage, Dispatchable Demand and Non-Firm connections:  
Calls to accelerate LDES procurement/design and to clarify DSU/dispatchable consumption 
frameworks in coordination with infrastructure readiness, decarbonisation pathways and LEU 
growth – are seen by stakeholders as being prerequisites for hitting flexibility targets. In 
addition, industry engagement is required to promote non-firm connections and support 
growth in demand-side flexibility from heat and transport. 
 
Customer Participation, Activation & Equity:  
Several stakeholders flagged low smart tariff adoption and a need for targeted 
engagement/support for vulnerable users and renters (e.g., education, access to meters, 
Building Energy Rating (BER) related constraints, accessing savings from smart tariffs). 
Consumer-centric technology and an approach to flexibility would enable mass adoption by 
tackling market complexity and cost inefficiency. Retail suppliers need to be included in the 
development of flexibility to support market access for customers and to be able to manage 
balancing risks arising from greater use of flexibility. 
 
Execution Discipline and Coordination:  
There were recurrent stakeholder asks for sharper prioritisation, timelines, accountability and 
coherent programme governance across CRU, SOs, and policy makers. Stakeholders noted 
that having multiple workstreams and programmes with overlapping objectives, similar 
timescales, and involving a common group of objectives creates a potential for confusion and 
inefficiency. Without the appropriate coordination, visibility of activities across programmes 
and policy alignment the progress towards decarbonisation and flexibility goals may be 
hindered.  
1.1.3 Additional themes of note: 
 
Updated NEDS: 
The majority of stakeholders (15 responses) were in favour of an update being made to the 
NEDS. Proposed revised scope items included provisions to reflect the LEAP, the LEU 
Connection Policy decision, storage policy, energy sharing/private wires, and evolving

20 
 
Corporate Power Purchase Agreements (CPPAs) / Guarantees of Origin (GO) / emissions 
transparency work.  
Many stakeholders indicated a preference for the application of key performance indicators 
(KPIs) and a single, system-level implementation roadmap that would sequence 
dependencies and clarify accountability.  
Only a minority of stakeholders sought no project scope changes at all, preferring delivery to 
continue to be against the current plan with frequent progress tracking. 
1.1.4 Summary 
Taking the opportunity to provide feedback, representatives from a number of stakeholder groups 
have responded to the NEDS Review Survey. Respondents noted that the NEDS has made good 
progress on smart metering and smart services area of actions and sent the right signals to the 
market through progress in flexibility procurement initiatives. However, respondents also noted 
that uncertainty of outcomes and delays in actions addressing key enablers for flexibility may pose 
a risk to the delivery of flexibility at scale. These comments are being taken into account for the 
rebaselining of actions and inform the approach to NEDS update. 
1.7 Demand Flexibility Forecasting Report 2026: 
NEDS Action 0.3 (CRU202629) 
As per NEDS Action 0.3: NEDS Progress reporting, the CRU is responsible for assessing the 
NEDS progress in three ways: (i) by estimating the flexibility associated with NEDS initiatives, (ii) 
tracking progress of actions, and (iii) reviewing the impact of NEDS actions on carbon emissions. 
As required by this action, the CRU will be publishing a Demand Flexibility Forecasting Report 
2026: NEDS Action 0.3 (CRU202629) shortly after this NEDS Annual Update 2026 publication. 
The report will present an estimate of demand-side flexibility, together with a description of the 
methodology and assumptions upon which such an estimate has been based. The tracking of 
carbon emissions is separately addressed within this publication both in the update provided for 
Action 0.2: Review the impact of NEDS on Carbon Emissions, in the table in Section 5 and also 
in the closing summary for the relevant action contained in the Appendix.  
1.8 CRU Large Energy Users Connection Policy 
Decision  
The CRU published the Large Energy Users Connection Policy Decision (CRU2025236) in 
December 2025. The purpose of this decision paper was to set out a pathway for new data centre

21 
 
applications to the electricity system to address risks in relation to security of supply and system 
constraints and promote renewable energy targets, while minimising, where possible, the impact 
on national carbon emissions. 
In recent years, there has been a step-change in electricity demand growth driven by LEUs, largely 
driven by the increase in data centre developments. Ireland’s total electricity demand has grown 
by 30% over the past 10 years, with data centre demand having greatly contributed to this level 
of growth. Accordingly, new data centres connecting under this policy will be required to provide 
new renewable and dispatchable electricity generation. The additional investment associated with 
these projects will help to address renewable energy targets and security of supply in the context 
of the additional demand associated with new data centres. 
This decision paper set out the CRU’s decisions in relation to the LEUs connection policy review 
and included a new direction to the electricity SOs under Section 34 of the 1999 Electricity 
Regulation Act. This direction supersedes Direction CRU/21/124 and will apply to all new 
connection applications for new or additional capacity captured under the scope of the decision. 
1.9 Smart Meter Data Access Code Decision 
To date, the National Smart Metering Programme (NSMP) has facilitated the nation-wide 
installation of more than 2.1 million smart meters. The new technology installed in smart meters 
allows for information on customers usage of electricity to be sent electronically from the smart 
meter to their respective electricity supplier and their actual electricity consumption is used to 
calculate their bill. This information is referred to as smart meter data.  
The CRU published its decision on the Smart Meter Data Access Code (SMDAC) on the 19th 
February 2025. This sets out how parties can access the data collected by smart meters and the 
rules around that access in addition to the CRU’s approach to governing the collection, retention, 
and utilisation of smart meter data. The introduction of the SMDAC will ensure that smart meter 
data is handled in an appropriate way, in accordance with all relevant data protection legislation.  
Suppliers and others must comply with the rules set out in the SMDAC and their obligations under 
data protection regulations before they can access smart meter data.  
Ultimately, the SMDAC will enable suppliers and others to deliver value to customers through the 
development and introduction of new smart services and products. The provision of smart meter 
data will create opportunities to offer additional services to customers, such as more accurate and 
personalised price comparisons, better tailored tariffs, and analysis of customers’ energy 
consumption. In addition, the provision of smart meter data under the SMDAC will also support 
the operation of the electricity network, helping Ireland to meet its climate action targets. It seeks

1.11 EirGrid Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES) 
Development  
Long duration energy storage (LDES) procurement in Ireland is being progressed by EirGrid to 
support the delivery of increased system flexibility and security as renewable penetration grows. 
The objective is to procure storage assets with extended duration (typically ≥4 hours) capable of 
shifting energy across time, reducing curtailment and redispatch, and providing system support 
services during periods of low renewable output. 
Since the previous NEDS biannual update, progress has advanced from early-stage options 
development to formal procurement design and consultation. Initial Call for Evidence work 
undertaken in 2023 and policy direction set through the 2024 Electricity Storage Policy Framework 
(including a mandate to procure up to 500 MW of LDES) have been followed by publication of an 
LDES procurement consultation in October 2025 and ongoing development of contract and 
evaluation frameworks throughout 2026. This reflects a transition from policy development to 
delivery phase, with the first procurement round expected to launch in 2027 and initial assets 
targeted to be operational by 2030.

2.1 Flexibility Needs Assessment 
The CRU has commenced Ireland’s first National Flexibility Needs Assessment (FNA), a new 
EU‑mandated process to understand how much electricity system flexibility Ireland will need, 
where it will be needed, and when, as the system transitions to high levels of renewable 
generation. The FNA covers both system‑wide needs and local network needs on the 
transmission and distribution networks. It is being delivered in collaboration with EirGrid and 
ESBN, using a common methodology approved by ACER to ensure consistency across Europe. 
The findings will help inform the setting of Ireland’s national non-fossil flexibility targets, support 
more efficient planning for renewable integration, guide future flexibility procurement frameworks, 
and support security of supply objectives.  
Progress has been made to date on the FNA, with the scope of the data and modelling agreed 
and detailed analysis currently underway by the SOs, targeting the delivery of Ireland’s first FNA 
report in Q3 2026. Alongside technical modelling, the FNA also includes a joint assessment of 
market barriers to flexibility, examining whether current market arrangements, signals and 
regulations enable flexibility to come forward where it is most valuable. This work will identify 
where barriers exist, where they are already being addressed, and where further policy or 
regulatory action may be required to help enable flexibility needs to be met efficiently by the 
market. 
2.2 Demand Response 
Previously, ACER initiated a consultation process and engaged with stakeholders on the 
proposed EU-wide network code on demand response (DRNC). The CRU, along with other 
National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs), contributed input throughout this engagement, which was 
then submitted by ACER to the EC on the 7th March 2025 for comitology (the process by which 
the EC implements EU law with the assistance of committees composed of national 
representatives). Formal adoption via comitology is expected during 2026. The scope of the Code 
includes rules to enable demand-side flexibility to participate in electricity markets on a non-
discriminatory and technology-neutral basis, including through aggregation, market access, 
coordination with SOs and principles for market-based procurement, and therefore aligns with the 
objective of NEDS to enable growth of flexibility. The CRU is currently planning the implementation 
of the Code, pending the outcomes of the comitology process, and will continue to monitor 
progress.

6. Next Steps  
 
The NEDS remains in its current implementation phase, with this publication representing the third 
update in the series. One further update is expected, which will provide a final consolidated 
position on delivery and support the close-out of this phase of the strategy. 
Significant progress has been made to date in advancing the delivery of NEDS actions and 
establishing the key building blocks required to enable demand-side flexibility. As implementation 
has progressed, the delivery environment has become increasingly complex, reflecting growing 
interdependencies with wider Government policy, infrastructure planning, and evolving European 
frameworks. 
In the period ahead, the CRU will continue to: 
• 
Monitor and report on progress against NEDS actions, including through the final 
planned update in this series; 
• 
Publish the Demand Flexibility Forecasting Report 2026: NEDS Action 0.3 
(CRU202629), providing an updated estimate of demand-side flexibility and the underlying 
methodology; 
• 
Engage with Government Departments, SOs, and other stakeholders, to reflect 
implementation experience and emerging developments across the energy system; 
• 
Support consideration of relevant EU developments, including the FNA and DRNC, 
as these progress. 
As set out in this update, a number of factors are shaping the delivery context for NEDS actions, 
including increasing demand growth, particularly from LEUs, and the continued development of 
national and European policy frameworks. These developments highlight the importance of 
ongoing coordination across relevant bodies, particularly where delivery relies on interactions 
between policy, regulatory, and operational functions. 
Looking beyond the current implementation phase, it is recognised that the next iteration of the 
NEDS will require a broader governance model, reflecting the fact that many of the key levers 
for enabling demand flexibility sit beyond the CRU’s regulatory remit. The development of a future 
strategy will therefore require cross-government ownership, with clearly defined roles, 
responsibilities, and coordination mechanisms across relevant departments and agencies. The 
CRU will continue to contribute its experience and insights from the delivery of the NEDS to inform 
this evolving discussion.

42 
 
In parallel, key areas of focus for the remainder of this implementation phase include: 
• Ensuring the delivery of remaining NEDS actions in line with revised timelines; 
• Advancing key enabling measures, including tariff development, flexibility 
procurement, and customer participation; 
• Maintaining visibility of dependencies and interactions across related programmes 
and policy initiatives. 
Overall, the focus for the next phase may increasingly involve moving from the delivery of 
individual actions towards achieving measurable flexibility outcomes at a system level, 
ensuring that Ireland’s energy demand can respond effectively to increasing renewable generation 
and evolving system needs. 
The CRU welcomes feedback (energydemandstrategy@cru.ie) in relation to the information set 
out in this NEDS Annual Update publication, or any topics relevant to the overall strategy.

A.1 NEDS Action 0.2: Review the impact of NEDS on 
carbon emissions (CRU) 
Following the completion of an initial scoping review, an information gathering approach was 
adopted to determine how best to adequately assess the effect of demand-side flexibility on grid 
carbon emissions and the contribution of NEDS actions.  
The CRU engaged firstly with MaREI where a qualitative and quantitative approach to account for 
indirect and enabling NEDS actions was discussed. Thereafter, the CRU engaged with DCEE and 
DETE where it was suggested that actions should be grouped by sector and compared to existing 
reporting frameworks as existing approaches to measuring carbon emissions (e.g. for CAP 
reporting) might not be sufficiently granular in order to adequately demonstrate the impact from 
NEDS actions. Finally, the CRU engaged with the SEAI and the EPA to assess the existing 
availability of data and modelling capabilities in order to accurately quantify the impact of NEDS 
actions. This engagement firstly highlighted the importance of the need for counterfactual 
modelling against which all calculations can be compared i.e. to quantify what the carbon 
emissions would otherwise be in the absence of the NEDS actions. Secondly, it became clear that 
challenges currently exist preventing the attribution of a measured impact to a specific NEDS 
action plus the necessary accessibility to more granular data - while assistance would be 
forthcoming to aid in the assessment of emissions calculations in general, the necessary data 
required to drive this is not currently available.  
In parallel, NEDS actions were reviewed and categorised to identify their potential impact on 
carbon emissions and relevance of the action to any such impact. For example: a direct change

44 
 
in emissions as a result of the action (Scope 2 emissions), an indirect impact on emissions (e.g. 
reduction in electricity consumption that requires fossil fuel to generate), or an enabling impact for 
actions that facilitate other emission-impacting measures. Once these initial steps had been 
completed, the next stage of the approach would then consist of identifying an appropriate 
methodology for quantifying the impact of each action category with sufficient granularity to assess 
the impact on the grid carbon emissions. 
The CRU’s initial review concluded that available data and its granularity are currently not 
sufficient to enable the quantification of the impacts of NEDS actions on carbon emissions.  In 
addition, having due regard to the requirements of Section 15 of the Climate Action and Low 
Carbon Development Act 2015 and the CRU’s existing statutory functions, it is recommended that 
it would be more appropriate for this action to be progressed as part of the next iteration of the 
NEDS with a reassignment of the action to responsible bodies possessing the necessary authority 
and functions, aligning with the key recommendations for Government Departments as contained 
in the NEDS Decision.  
Ultimately the next phase should focus on refining the CRU’s initial approach, securing data 
access, and ensuring governance structures are in place to deliver a robust and transparent 
framework to enable the measurement of the carbon impact of NEDS actions into the future.

This action mandated suppliers to undertake market testing, research, and trials to enable the 
development of tariff products suited to business customer demand profiles. Commercial and 
industrial customers operate under load profiles materially distinct from domestic consumption,

domestic tariff offering. Action 1.8 is now complete, with evidence showing that the majority of 
suppliers offer multiple tariff options tailored to the operational needs of different commercial and 
industrial customers and the required market testing, research, and trials have been undertaken

now available to commercial and industrial customers. The developed products reflect segment-
differentiated design, demand response elements, and design informed by commercial and 
industrial load profiles demonstrating that the intended market capability has been 
established. Suppliers have incorporated insights obtained from testing and trials into product 
design, and businesses now have access to tariff structures that are adapted to and better reflect 
their consumption patterns.

practices, global standards, and DER control architectures. ESBN complemented this with internal 
technical assessments, including smart inverter testbeds, proofs of concept, and a nationwide 
field pilot using the IEEE 2030.5 communication protocol to test end to end DER controllability. 
The pilot involved real sites where ESBN deployed gateways, Modbus integrations, and 
communication interfaces to validate monitoring, curtailment, voltage control, and EV charging 
control. This combined desk based, lab, and field-based methodology ensured that technical 
recommendations were based on both analysis and practical deployment evidence. 
Throughout the development of action 1.16, ESBN engaged regularly with the CRU to provide 
regular updates on progress. In addition, ESBN also engaged directly with DCEE as chair of the 
Smart Energy Services Working Group (SESWG) and the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland 
(SEAI).  
The action produced a comprehensive technical whitepaper, a detailed network pilot performance 
report, and a set of recommended technical requirements for small scale solar PV and storage 
systems. The pilot successfully demonstrated Ireland’s first IEEE 2030.5 based utility control of 
rooftop PV, proving reliable telemetry, curtailment, voltage control, and EV charging management. 
These findings directly inform updates to ESBN standards, communication protocol requirements, 
and the future DER control architecture needed for flexibility markets.  
ESBN provided a comprehensive briefing to ESBN’s Advisory Council in November 2025 outlining 
the background and context to the action, the development of the network pilot, pilot findings and 
basis for further work. The final ESBN report outlining the key findings and recommendations was 
submitted to the CRU in May 2026.

A.20 NEDS Action 2.15: European SCALE project 
monitoring (CRU) 
Project Smart Charging Alignment for Europe (SCALE) is a Horizon 2020 project which was 
running for three years and was concluded at the end of 2025. Its aim was to advance smart

56 
 
charging infrastructure and facilitate the mass deployment of EVs by identifying and reducing 
technical, organisational, economic, and policy barriers. Based on a collection of use-cases 
across EU, Project SCALE demonstrates that smart charging and V2X technologies are 
technically viable and can enable EVs to act as distributed flexibility resources, but their large-
scale deployment is constrained primarily by system-level factors rather than technology. Across 
its workstreams, SCALE shows that user behaviour (requiring automation and simplicity), 
fragmented stakeholder roles, lack of interoperability standards, and limited market access for 
aggregated EV flexibility are key barriers.  
SCALE provides clear evidence that EVs can become a significant source of demand-side 
flexibility, but only if regulatory frameworks enable participation in multiple markets, stream line 
aggregation, and value stacking. It also reinforces the need to prioritise fleet-led deployment, 
interoperability standards, and “smart-by-default” consumer approaches to unlock participation at 
scale. Importantly, the project highlights that EV integration must be treated as a whole-system 
challenge, requiring alignment between distribution network planning, transport policy, and 
flexibility market design. For each barrier area, Project SCALE provides a list of lessons learned 
and identified barriers for accelerating Smart EV charging and vehicle-to-anything bidirectional 
charging which could help informing the focus of the NEDS update. 
In parallel, CRU have been monitoring developments and initiatives in policy, and consultations 
on NEDS related topics, including from ACER, individual Member States and the EC.
